I think the non-reproducible behavior about the NULL values was because earlier I was still using the master branch that dealt with issue #26. With version 2.2.0 the problem is gone.

About the NAs, I do not have a strong opinion. Currently I don't see a reason why the NAs should be kept by split. So the current way rmr handles this (i.e. dropping the NAs) is fine with me. Overriding split's behavior is probably not worth the performance penalty you have to pay (not even speaking about making the code more complicated to maintain and extend).

Nonetheless, in case I later come across a compelling reason why the NAs should be kept, I'll let you know.

> This happens because keys are used for grouping. Grouping is done with split and split drops NA's (undocumented)
> ```
> > split(2:3, c(1, NA))
> $`1`
> [1] 2
> ```
> I've already overridden split's behavior in a couple of cases, but there's a performance penalty to pay.  Do you think split should just treat NA as another value? The problem is that NA == NA is not true, is NA, so one has to special case the NAs.
>
>
> Antonio
>
> On Monday, April 29, 2013 10:19:46 PM UTC-7, Antonio Piccolboni wrote:
> > Strange for the non reproducible error, those are the toughest ones. As far as the NA behavior that's not what I expected,  I will think about it but it seems like a bug to me.
> >
> >
> > Antonio
> >
> >
> > On Mon, Apr 29, 2013 at 7:37 PM, Michael Smith <my.r...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > > > So after trying various cases, I found out the following result:
> > > > > If I try use NULL keys, it does not work to selectively drop records, since I get the error message, "can't mix NULL and not NULL key keyval pairs."
> > > > What you may be doing is mixing keyval(1,10) and keyval(NULL, 10). That is something I decided to disallow when it tightened the semantics for keyval related operations following some bug reports and requests for clarfication.
> > >
> > > Yes, keyval(NULL, 10) is what I meant by 'NULL keys', the way I understand the first table in your link <https://github.com/RevolutionAnalytics/RHadoop/wiki/Keyval-types-and-combinations>, since it is key=NULL and value=(length>0). By the way, I'm fine with this design choice, I just wanted to report what worked and what didn't work for me when trying to drop some records.
> > >
> > > > > If I use 0-length keyval for the records I want to drop, I don't get an error message, but for the records I do want to keep, there is a problem. In particular, for the records I do want to keep, I use return(keyval(x, y)), where y is a 1 by 2 matrix. However, while rmr keeps the first column of that matrix, it drops the second column of that matrix, although I would like to keep that column.
> > > > That's a bug and needs to be fixed, please provide a test case.
> > >
> > > Strange, today I cannot reproduce this any more. If I use return(NULL) (which is according to my understanding does the same as return(keyval(NULL, NULL))), the record gets dropped and the for the records I want to keep, the second column of the matrix is not discarded. > > >
> > > >
> > > > > The "normal case" does work, where I use return(keyval(NA, y)) for the records I want to discard, and return(keyval(x, y)) for the records I want to keep.
> > > > That is not filtering, you can do it, but it doesn't discard any records unless you later check for NA and discard them. I would call it a workaround at best.
> > >
> > > Actually, the NAs do get dropped when I run the following code, and I don't have to remove the NAs later:
> > >
> > > library("rmr2")
> > > rmr.options(backend = "local")
> > > rmr.options(keyval.length = 2)
> > > mapper <- function(k, v) {
> > >   if(sum(v) < 15) {                     # Return 'normal case'.
> > >     return(keyval(1, v))
> > >   } else {                              # Return 'NA key'.
> > >     return(keyval(NA, v))
> > >   }
> > > }
> > > output <- mapreduce(to.dfs(keyval(1:10)), map = mapper)
> > > from.dfs(output)
> > >
> > > I do agree though that it would be better to use your example from your previous post, which returns NULL in case we don't want to keep the record.

messages.body_plain:
Actually, I think you have done a wonderful job integrating Hadoop with R. They key point is that everything is very R-like, so that you can wrap MapReduce jobs into function calls, then pass the results to other functions, loop around them, and so forth. Essentially one does not have the feeling that one is doing something outside of R, while in fact one is working with Hadoop behind the scenes, which is obviously quite different than R. So to integrate all of this together, and do it in an elegant way is a remarkable feat.

Also, the local backend is incredibly useful. This is for two reasons. First, you can debug your MapReduce code with so much ease, it's almost frightening. In particular, to insert select calls to browser in the mapper or reducer worlks wonders; not only for debugging, but also for writing new code. In particular, it makes it very easy to see what's going on inside the mapper and reducer. Without the local backend, it would be a lot more difficult, since the mapper and reducer would not be running "inside R," but in a separate process. The second reason is that it's much faster to use the local backend. When submitting a job to Hadoop, it always takes a few seconds until it even starts running, and then again a few seconds until everything is cleand up after the job finishes. In contrast, with the local backend, it reacts instantaneously, which makes it much faster to improve your code. Of course, with the local backend, one can only use it on small example data, but that's completely OK, since once the program works on the small example data set, it is relatively easy to switch back to the Hadoop backend and run it on the big data.

To give you an example how easy it is to use RHadoop, my team and I have created a relatively large project using Hadoop Streaming and R. It took months to get it running properly, since so many details had to be explicitly taken care of. (The long duration to write the code might also have been a function of our inexperience with Hadoop.) But I found it shocking that I was able to re-implement a large portion of that project in RHadoop (in particular rmr) over the last few days. So what once took us months to write was possible to be rewritten in days using RHadoop. (Again, this might to some extent be a function of us being now more experienced with Hadoop, but I don't think tha'ts the whole story and that still rmr is much nicer to work with).

I also find it very encouraging that Antonio is always very responsive. The minor problems I had so far with RHadoop led to two issues on the issue tracker, and both of them were fixed within a matter of hours.

To sum it up: many congratulations on writing such an outstanding piece of software, and keep up the good work!

mapreduce(input = dir-with-csv-files, output = dir-for-concatenated-files, map = function(k,v) cbind(fname = Sys.getenv("map_input_file"), input.format = make.input.format("csv", other-args-to-read.table))

This error happens when R is not installed or not properly installed on one or more nodes. Rscript should be executable from any directory, which means installed into a directory in the PATH variable. Normally jobs are executed under a different user account than that of the person actually issuing the job, so you need to be sure that you make Rscript available to the right user, or every user, which is my usual approach. Also people sometimes configure only interactive shells changing the .bashrc file, but here we need to configure also non interactive or batch shells, using the .profile or .bash_profile files. I hope this helps

Antonio

messages.subject: Re: RCFile Format
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
you need to create an input format for RCfile. In rmr2 parlance, an input format is created with
make.input.format(
  rmr2:::make.typedbytes.input.format(),
  "binary",
  streaming.format = "org.apache.hadoop.hive.ql.io.rcfileinputformat")

You can see I am reusing a private function, so we are stretching the flexibility of the IO subsystem of rmr2 a bit, but I think it's OK for an experiment, we may fix it later. Whether this works or not depends on, among other things, how well the data model of the RCfile format maps to typedbytes, a simplified serialization format for sending data to non-java programs. People using this approach to read Hive tables have run into problems because of the slightly different implementation of typedbytes therein. Let me know if you have additional questions and if the approach work out.

Antonio

messages.subject: MapR Support for rmr2
messages.body_plain:
I have struggled with building and installing the rmr2 package on MapR.  MapR is fast becoming popular as a robust high availability Hadoop platform.  Unfortunately, the rmr2 build script doesn't work well for a MapR Hadoop installation.  Luckily all the problems were in the shell script src/hbase-io/build_linux.sh.  There were 2 kinds of differences:
Incorrect wildcard patterns or paths for jar files
Searching for an explicit version of apache-ant.  The version 1.8.4 is no longer available at the location searched.
Here are the differences between my script and the one in the official rmr2 package:

160,162c160,162
<     if [ ! -e apache-ant-1.9.0 ]; then
<         wget http://mirror.nus.edu.sg/apache/ant/binaries/apache-ant-1.9.0-bin.tar.gz
<         tar zxf apache-ant-1.9.0-bin.tar.gz
---
>     if [ ! -e apache-ant-1.8.4 ]; then
>         wget http://mirror.nus.edu.sg/apache/ant/binaries/apache-ant-1.8.4-bin.tar.gz
>         tar zxf apache-ant-1.8.4-bin.tar.gz
164c164
<     export PATH=apache-ant-1.9.0/bin:$PATH
---
>     export PATH=apache-ant-1.8.4/bin:$PATH
207,211c207,210
< # JVR - Fixed test to check in lib folder
< if ls ${hadoop_path}/lib/hadoop-*-core.jar; then
<     cp ${hadoop_path}/lib/hadoop-*-core.jar ./lib/
< elif ls ${hadoop_path}/lib/hadoop-core-*.jar; then
<     cp ${hadoop_path}/lib/hadoop-core-*.jar ./lib/

>     cp ${hadoop_path}/hadoop-*-core.jar ./lib/
> elif ls ${hadoop_path}/hadoop-core-*.jar; then
>     cp ${hadoop_path}/hadoop-core-*.jar ./lib/

messages.body_plain:
rmr2 picks whatever configuration hadoop has. So if you set the env variable HADOOP_CMD to /usr/loca/bin/hadoop and when you use that command, it runs in standalone mode, rmr2 will run in standalone mode. Same for distributed and pseudodistributed modes. So I would first make sure that HADOOP_CMD is pointing where you expect and then look up the documentation for CDH4 searching  for "configure distributed mode". I am sure also there are Cloudera user forums and Hadoop user forums where you will find better answers than here. But if you configure Hadoop right and rmr is using the Hadoop copy that you think it is using (this is a problem if you have multiple hadoop installed, like I do) rmr2 doesn't have any additional configuration. Of course there is the backend choice, but rmr starts on the hadoop backend by default and that doesn't sound like your problem. Just to be super cautions, you could check rmr.options("backend") . It should return "hadoop". I hope this helps

Antonio

You need to install rmr2 and all its dependencies on each node of the cluster. If you've done that already, you may have a problem like in that thread that R doesn't find them, and that's an issue with users and directories. I always recommend installing packages for every user in the most standard locations. People who diligently follow instructions for an unprivileged install need to realize that they may have user account johnstat, but the jobs and hence map process hence R interpreter is going to run as user hadoop or mapred, a dedicated user created by the hadoop install process. That requires a modified .libPaths in R. There is no special feature to set that in rmr2 but it should be possible using standard R configuration files. That's as much as I know about it. Of course I would encourage anybody to do a standard install for every user, that way one install serves many people, everyone is happier in the long run.
